source.title: Double Descent in Portfolio Optimization: Dance between Theoretical Sharpe Ratio and Estimation Accuracy
source.authors: Yong-He Lu; Yan-Rong Yang; Terry Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. Some equations and symbols are garbled in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the broad claim that risk can improve again beyond an interpolation threshold, using portfolio models and portfolio prediction loss rather than deep-network test error.
record.gate_note: The study's own theoretical, simulated, and empirical results are included below. References to double-descent results in other work are background only. The empirical study reports Sharpe ratios, not prediction loss; no epoch-wise or training-sample-size sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study derives and simulates out-of-sample prediction loss (an MSE-type risk) for a pseudoinverse (minimum-ℓ2-norm) mean-variance portfolio estimator. It varies N/T across the interpolation point ρ=1, so it bears on V4 in a new, non-deep-network model class. The real-data part reports only Sharpe ratios, which no version names. T3 fits better than T2: this is a new setting, not a different method aimed at deep-network double descent.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find a 'double ascent' in out-of-sample Sharpe ratio as the number of assets grows, analogous to double descent, plus a decrease in prediction loss once N exceeds T. They attribute the first ascent to the rising clairvoyant Sharpe ratio and the second to better estimation accuracy under minimum-ℓ2-norm inductive bias. The benefit grows with factor strength. Empirically the best high-dimensional model (Sharpe ~1.4) beats the best low-dimensional one (~0.8).
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes mean-variance portfolios with a generalized-inverse estimator, using asset count as complexity and Sharpe ratio or portfolio prediction loss as performance measures; it does not reproduce deep-network training or test-error measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Theoretical results vary with the asset-to-observation ratio and factor strength. The paper also studies a ridge-regularized estimator in the supplement, but does not report optimally tuned regularization eliminating the peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Out-of-sample Sharpe ratio shows a 'double ascent'. Empirically it peaks near N=39 (~0.8 annualized), dips near ρ_T=1, and rises to ~1.4 for N>450. In theory, at fixed θ̃ it rises past ρ=1 then declines again for large ρ. The equal-weighted portfolio is flat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sharpe-ratio performance of minimum-norm mean-variance portfolios is non-monotone in asset count, with a second ascent beyond N=T whose strength depends on factor structure.

record.problems: The paper's empirical exercise cannot evaluate its defined prediction-loss metric because the population parameters are unavailable, so the real-data evidence uses Sharpe ratios instead. The theoretical conclusions rely on stated asymptotic assumptions; the empirical replications are reported without confidence intervals or error bars.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results directly measuring prediction loss across separately reported settings were available in the text beyond the theoretical results and the aggregate simulation conclusion recorded above. Other empirical portfolio metrics in Table 1, including CER and minimum-variance portfolio results, are not direct measures of the claim's test-risk curve.

untested.parts: No deep networks; no model-size sweep of network test error.
No training-time or epoch axis; closed-form estimator.
T is fixed (100 in simulation, 120 or 60 empirically); no sample-size sweep reported as a result.
Only one model class (linear portfolio estimator). Real-data prediction loss is not measured.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
The ridge estimator in Supplement D gives only limit formulas, with no result on whether tuned regularization removes the peak. No noise manipulation and no multiple peaks.

missing.what: Prediction loss for ρ<1: rises monotonically toward the threshold (peak side of the curve).
Prediction loss in the 'mimicking real-world' scenario (θ increasing in N, T=100, ϕ̃ in {0,0.05,1,10,100}): descent in the overparameterized regime.
Theoretical Sharpe ratio curves (Theorems 1, 3) showing an ascent past ρ=1 and a later decline.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The headline 'double descent' is about Sharpe ratio, which no version names; only the prediction-loss theory and simulation bear on V4. The loss limit σ²(1+θ̃) equalling the zero-portfolio loss is our reading of Definition 2 and Theorem 2, not stated by the authors. Empirical replications have no confidence intervals.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error as model size grows.
Increasing training-sample size near the interpolation threshold.
Tests portfolio-model prediction loss, not risk across a range of AI model classes; the empirical exercise reports Sharpe ratio rather than prediction loss.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes it.
Whether an effective-parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: Pseudoinverse portfolio estimator under uncorrelated assets
rows.size_stated: N assets; complexity measured by N/T = ρ
rows.operation_detail: Asymptotic analysis as the asset-to-observation ratio ρ changes
rows.measure: Out-of-sample prediction loss, defined as squared distance from the true optimal portfolio return
rows.value: Prediction loss decreases as ρ increases in (1, ∞); its limit is σ²(1 + θ̃).
rows.locator: Section 3.1.2, Theorem 2 and discussion of Figure 3
rows.note: The paper describes this as a decrease in prediction loss in the over-parameterized range.
rows.check: State is correct for ρ>1. The row omits the ρ<1 side of Theorem 2: loss rises as ρ→1, giving a peak at the threshold. It also omits that, at fixed θ̃, the loss only falls toward σ²(1+θ̃) and shows no first descent.

source_check.correct: Loss decreases beyond the interpolation singularity and converges to σ²(1+θ̃). Monotone decrease throughout (1,∞) is too strong: algebraically, Equation (7) approaches that limit from below for the θ̃ values plotted, implying an eventual increase.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1.2, Theorem 2, Equation (7), Figures 3–4; Appendix C.2 loss expansion.
source_check.problem: The row turns a decrease within the overparameterized range into an unrestricted monotonicity claim.

rows.subject: Pseudoinverse portfolio estimator under the single-factor model
rows.size_stated: N assets; complexity measured by N/T = ρ
rows.operation_detail: Asymptotic analysis as the asset-to-observation ratio ρ and factor strength vary
rows.value: Prediction loss decreases in the over-parameterized range; the paper states that stronger factors produce lower prediction loss in the large-ρ regime.
rows.locator: Section 3.2.2, Theorem 4 and discussion of Figures 7–8
rows.note: The result is asymptotic and conditional on the stated factor-model assumptions.
rows.check: Correct. Note that the ρ<1 limit is identical to the no-factor case (Remark 1), so factor strength matters only past the threshold.

source_check.correct: Theorem 4 gives post-interpolation loss recovery; the accompanying text states that stronger factors lower prediction loss in the large-ρ regime. Decrease throughout the entire overparameterized range is not general: at ϕ̃=0, Equation (12) reduces to the nonmonotonic Equation (7).
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.2, Theorem 4, Equation (12), paragraph preceding Figure 7 and Figures 7–8.
source_check.problem: The unqualified decrease over the overparameterized range needs narrowing; the factor-strength statement is supported.

rows.subject: Simulated pseudoinverse portfolio estimator
rows.operation_detail: Finite-sample simulation across asset counts and signal-to-noise ratios

conditions.value: 1000 times for each combination of ρ_T and ϕ

rows.value: The finite-sample simulations are reported as validating the consistency of the theoretical results; Figure 11 plots finite-sample and asymptotic performance.
rows.note: The text reports the aggregate conclusion, not separate numerical prediction-loss values for each plotted condition.
rows.check: subject_kind 'toy_network' is wrong: this is a simulated portfolio estimator, not a network. The value is the authors' aggregate statement that simulations match the asymptotic curves; no per-condition loss numbers can be read.

rows.subject: U.S. equity characteristic-ranked portfolio models using the pseudoinverse estimator
rows.size_stated: N varied from 2 to 696 in the reported table; the sweep uses 151 N values up to 700
rows.operation_detail: Out-of-sample portfolio evaluation as the number of assets changes
rows.value: The average Sharpe ratio peaks around ρ_T = 0.3250 (N = 39), reaches a minimum near ρ_T = 1, then rises and stabilizes around 1.4 for ρ_T > 1.
rows.uncertainty: 100 replications are shown; no confidence interval or error-bar value is stated.
rows.note: This is a Sharpe-ratio performance curve, not test error or the prediction-loss measure named by V4.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The Sharpe ratio is not a risk/test-error measure; the authors say prediction loss is infeasible on real data.

rows.subject: Equal-weighted portfolio
rows.operation_detail: Equal-weighted portfolio performance as the number of assets changes
rows.measure: Sharpe ratio and certainty equivalent return
rows.value: Both are almost constant across different numbers of assets; the paper notes a slight improvement when N is small.
rows.note: These portfolio-performance measures do not directly measure the risk curve specified in the claim.
rows.check: This is a comparator baseline (1/N portfolio) on Sharpe/CER, not a measure of any version. It is arguably not a result row at all.

relationships.reason: Prediction loss blows up as ρ→1 and decreases for ρ>1 in both theory (r1, r2), and simulations match the theory (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Prediction loss diverged as ρ→1 and decreased for ρ>1 under both return models, with simulations matching theory.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Asymptotic theory (uncorrelated and single-factor returns) and finite-sample simulations, T=100, pseudoinverse estimator
source_check.reason: Theorems 2 and 4 show divergent loss near interpolation and recovery beyond it; Section 3.4 compares simulations with the asymptotic curves. This supports recovery without establishing indefinite monotone improvement.

relationships.condition: Fixed clairvoyant Sharpe ratio θ̃ (Theorems 2 and 4)
relationships.reason: Loss is lowest at small ρ and rises toward ρ=1 with no first descent (r1). Past ρ=1 it falls only toward σ²(1+θ̃). Under Definition 2 that equals the zero-weight portfolio's loss (our derivation), so the second descent never beats low complexity. Its size depends on factor strength ϕ̃ (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Loss rose toward ρ=1 before falling toward σ²(1+θ̃), the derived zero-weight portfolio loss, with recovery magnitude depending on ϕ̃.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Fixed clairvoyant Sharpe ratio θ̃ (Theorems 2 and 4)
source_check.reason: At fixed θ̃, low-ρ loss rises from zero rather than exhibiting an initial descent, qualifying the full double-descent shape. The supplied rationale needs correction: convergence to the zero-weight loss does not mean loss stays above it; Equation (7) can approach that limit from below. Outperforming low complexity is not itself required by V4.
